source.title: UNICORN on RAINBOW: A Universal Commonsense Reasoning Model on a New Multitask Benchmark
source.authors: Nicholas Lourie; Ronan Le Bras; Chandra Bhagavatula; Yejin Choi

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling-law work to justify a monotonicity assumption for its cost-equivalent curves, but its experiments assess transfer learning rather than scaling-law claims about language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The paper states that performance is empirically monotonic with parameters, compute, and data, citing Kaplan et al.; it does not test power-law loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its own measurements concern task accuracy and transfer data efficiency. The adjacent finding about model size and transfer benefit is recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to justify a monotonicity assumption behind cost-equivalent curves and in related work. It neither tests scaling-law claims nor depends on power-law results. Its experiments measure fine-tuning transfer and data efficiency on commonsense tasks with T5. The three-size transfer comparison concerns transfer benefit, not loss scaling or downstream predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that cost equivalent curves usefully compare data efficiency. They also conclude that sequential training rarely hurts, that RAINBOW transfers best for common sense, and that larger models benefit more from transfer. UNICORN sets SOTA on 8 benchmarks. They treat scaling as reliable motivation, not something they test.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or directly test the original scaling-law method; it studies transfer learning and uses a cited monotonicity result to motivate its evaluation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that transfer outcomes vary with model size, training recipe, data amount, and source dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger T5 models gain more data efficiency from RAINBOW transfer to CommonsenseQA, with gradient updates held fixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The data-efficiency benefit of intermediate-task transfer grows with pretrained model size.

record.problems: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss or test scaling laws. Its model-size transfer result is qualitative, with no numerical savings stated in the text; the investigatory results are reported on dev sets.
record.rows_left_out: No scaling-law results are reported. Other transfer and benchmark results do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No shape variation at fixed parameters.
No power-law fits in fine-tuning or other regimes.
Downstream accuracy rises with T5 size (Table 26), but only three sizes, no predictive fit or loss link.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'uses_without_test'/T4 is changed to cites_only/T6. The Kaplan citation only justifies a monotonicity assumption for isotonic regression. No reported result depends on scaling laws.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger-run losses from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of training compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.

rows.subject: T5-SMALL, T5-BASE, and T5-LARGE (aggregate comparison)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained T5; subsequently fine-tuned for transfer
rows.operation_detail: Compared transfer from RAINBOW to COMMONSENSE QA across model sizes.

conditions.value: model size; number of gradient updates held fixed

rows.measure: Transfer benefit in cost-equivalent curves, described as examples saved relative to the relevant single-task baselines.
rows.baseline: Single-task baselines; no numerical baseline value stated.
rows.value: The authors report that larger models seem to benefit more from transfer and save more examples; no numerical values stated.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative trend stated by the authors across the three model sizes; the figure is not accompanied by extractable numerical savings. This measures transfer benefit by model size, not downstream performance predictability from scale.
rows.check: Measures transfer data-efficiency gain across three T5 sizes (60M–770M), not loss vs scale or downstream predictability. The state 'observed' has no claim version to refer to. The value is qualitative only. Tables 26–27 give per-size accuracies but no fit.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
